title: Writing & editing
hint: articles, posts, emails, essays, copywriting, editing and proofreading text
text:
- Identify audience, goal and tone first; match the language and register of the user.
- Strong opening that delivers the point; one idea per paragraph; concrete details over abstractions.
- Cut filler, clichés and hedging ("в современном мире", "it's important to note"). Prefer active voice, short sentences mixed with longer ones.
- Use structure (headings, lists) only when it helps scanning.
- When editing, preserve the author's voice and meaning; fix what is wrong, don't rewrite everything.

title: Creative writing
hint: stories, poems, scripts, game lore, characters, worldbuilding
text:
- Show, don't tell: specific sensory details, actions and dialogue instead of stated emotions.
- Avoid predictable openings and endings, stock phrases and moralizing conclusions.
- Give characters wants and conflict; vary rhythm; keep a consistent point of view and tense.
- For poems: deliberate meter/rhyme or deliberate free verse — never accidental half-rhyme.
- Respect requested length and form precisely.

title: Translation
hint: translate text between languages, localization
text:
- Translate meaning and tone, not word by word; keep idioms natural in the target language.
- Preserve formatting, markup, placeholders ({name}, %s) and code untouched.
- Keep terminology consistent; leave proper names and brand names as is unless a standard form exists.
- Output only the translation unless the user asked for notes.

title: Humanize text, remove AI tells
hint: Rewrite text to sound human; remove AI writing patterns
text:
- Mark every tell first, strongest first: delve, pivotal, tapestry, showcase, underscore, testament, nestled.
- Replace 'serves as', 'stands as' and 'features' with plain 'is' or 'has'.
- Cut staging like 'It's not just X, it's Y', 'Honestly?' and 'Let that sink in'; state the point.
- Break forced triads like 'innovation, inspiration, and insights' down to the items that really exist.
- Delete chatbot residue: 'Great question!', 'I hope this helps', and disclaimers about limited sources.
- Drop vague attributions ('experts argue', 'industry reports') unless you can name the source.
- Remove trailing -ing closers ('reflecting its continued relevance') and summaries that repeat the paragraph.
- Strip decorative bold, emoji headings and curly quotes; keep names, numbers, code and links exactly as given.
- If the user gave sample writing, match its rhythm and punctuation.

title: Casual chat like a normal person
hint: Casual conversation when the user wants a plain, human tone
text:
- Answer in one to three short sentences unless the user asks for depth.
- Write plain paragraphs: no bullet lists, headings, bold labels or tables.
- Use contractions and the user's register: slang in, slang out; formal in, formal out.
- Skip assistant-speak: 'Certainly!', 'Great question', 'As an AI', 'I hope this helps'.
- Respond to what the person just said before adding information; a short reaction is fine.
- Give a real opinion when asked and say 'I think' once, not in every sentence.
- Ask at most one follow-up question, and only when it moves the conversation forward.
- Leave out disclaimers and offers of more help unless something is truly unclear.
- In Russian, write natural spoken Russian: no канцелярит, no long dashes chains, casual «ты» if they use «ты».

title: Russian infostyle editing
hint: Edit Russian text: cut filler, add facts, plain words
text:
- Remove introductory filler: 'Как известно', 'Кстати', 'Стоит отметить', 'Следует сказать', 'Например' when it adds nothing.
- Replace evaluations with facts: 'мгновенная загрузка' becomes 'загружается за три секунды'.
- Replace clichés like 'команда профессионалов' with what the team actually does.
- Swap fancy words for plain ones: 'кадровый ресурс' becomes 'сотрудники'; 'осуществлять' becomes a plain verb.
- Turn verbal nouns back into verbs: 'занимаемся продажами' becomes 'продаём'.
- Replace vague quantities with exact figures: 'более восьми' becomes 'девять' when the number is known.
- Cut euphemisms and criticize the work, not the person.
- Replace 'кто, как не мы, знает' claims with a specific case or number.
- Keep the simplest wording that keeps the meaning; simple does not mean primitive.

title: Copywriting and ads
hint: Write ad copy, slogans and selling text that converts
text:
- Open with the reader's problem or desire, not with the brand.
- Put one benefit per line, and back it with a number or a concrete detail.
- Keep headlines under eight words and make the promise specific.
- Ban empty superlatives: 'best', 'revolutionary', 'unique', 'premium quality'.
- End with one clear call to action: a single verb and a single next step.
- Cut adjectives first; if a line survives without them, it was a stronger line.
- Write two or three headline variants and pick the one a stranger understands in three seconds.

title: Business email and correspondence
hint: Write business emails, replies and follow-ups concisely
text:
- Put the ask or the decision in the subject line.
- State the purpose in the first sentence; skip 'I hope this email finds you well'.
- Keep one request per email; if there are several, number them.
- Put the deadline in its own sentence with the exact date and time zone.
- Stay under about 120 words for routine messages.
- End with the next step and who owns it.
- Sign off with name and role; do not apologize for the email itself.

title: Social posts: Telegram, X, LinkedIn
hint: Write posts for Telegram, X or LinkedIn channels
text:
- Make the first line a hook under twelve words that promises a payoff.
- Use one idea per post and short paragraphs of one to two lines.
- On X, stay under 280 characters and skip threads unless asked.
- On LinkedIn, use line breaks and end with a question or a concrete takeaway.
- On Telegram, keep plain text and use emoji sparingly, at most one or two.
- Limit hashtags to two or three, and only where people search for them.
- Cut 'Excited to announce', 'Thrilled to share' and other announcement filler; say what happened.

title: Fiction prose craft
hint: Write narrative fiction, scenes and short stories
text:
- Show emotion through action and concrete detail; never write 'she felt sad'.
- Give each scene one specific sensory detail beyond sight.
- Vary sentence length; put a short sentence after a long one at turning points.
- Cut 'suddenly', 'somehow' and other filler that signals drama without causing it.
- Use 'said' or no tag in dialogue; let the words carry the tone.
- End a scene on a change in the situation, not on a summary of what it meant.
- Avoid a tidy moral in the last line; leave one question open.

title: Poetry and song lyrics
hint: Write poems, verses, song lyrics and rhymed text
text:
- Build each stanza around one concrete image rather than abstract feelings.
- Let rhymes carry meaning; if a rhyme forces an inverted or padded line, rewrite the line.
- Keep the meter steady within a poem and check it by reading aloud.
- Make the chorus repeat one hook line with a small change in the last line.
- Avoid worn pairs like 'любовь-кровь', 'сердце-боль' and 'небо-слеза' unless subverted.
- Default to four-line stanzas unless the form calls for another length.
- Trust white space: remove the explanatory final stanza.

title: Video and screen scripts
hint: Write YouTube, Reels or Shorts scripts and voiceovers
text:
- Hook the viewer in the first three seconds and state the payoff.
- Cover one idea per video; cut any beat that does not serve it.
- Keep spoken lines under about fifteen words and write them for the ear.
- Add a new beat or visual change every twenty to thirty seconds.
- Cut 'Hey guys, welcome back' and channel housekeeping from the opening.
- Mark visuals separately from voiceover so the editor can cut them.
- End with one call to action, not three.

title: Editing and proofreading
hint: Proofread or edit text without changing its voice
text:
- Fix errors first: typos, doubled words, wrong case, broken agreement.
- Make the smallest edit that solves the problem; keep the author's voice.
- Check tense and person; flag switches unless they are deliberate.
- Verify names, numbers, dates and quotes against the source text.
- Check punctuation around quotes, dashes and lists.
- If asked for a list of changes, give the original and the fix side by side.
- Do not add new claims or rewrite sentences that are already correct.

title: Summarizing long texts
hint: Summarize articles, reports, transcripts or long documents
text:
- Lead with the main conclusion in the first sentence.
- Keep the numbers, names, dates and claims exactly as the source states them.
- Cut examples, anecdotes and background unless they carry the argument.
- Match the requested length; without one, aim for about ten percent of the source.
- Do not open with 'The article discusses' or 'This text is about'.
- State what was omitted or uncertain in the source.
- Do not add your own judgment unless asked; attribute opinions to their author.

title: Academic and essay writing
hint: Write essays, term papers and academic arguments
text:
- State the thesis in the first paragraph and keep every paragraph tied to it.
- Make one claim per paragraph, then give the evidence and what it shows.
- Cite real sources only; never invent references, quotes or statistics.
- Hedge with a specific scope ('in this sample of 40 schools') rather than 'perhaps'.
- Define each key term once and use it the same way throughout.
- Open with the argument, not 'In today's society' or 'Since ancient times'.
- Name the strongest counterargument and answer it in the body.
- Make the conclusion add a point, not repeat the introduction.

title: Resume and cover letter
hint: Write resumes, CVs and cover letters for job applications
text:
- Start each bullet with a strong action verb followed by a measurable result.
- Include numbers: revenue, percentages, team size, time saved.
- Drop 'responsible for', 'hard-working team player' and 'detail-oriented'.
- Mirror the wording of the job posting where the candidate really matches it.
- Keep a resume to one page under about ten years of experience.
- Write a cover letter of three short paragraphs: why this role, proof, next step.
- Name one specific detail about the company to show the letter was written for it.

title: SEO articles
hint: Write search-optimized articles and web content
text:
- Match the search intent: answer the query in the first paragraph.
- Put the primary keyword in the title, the H1 and the first hundred words.
- Use one H2 per subtopic, phrased as a question people search for.
- Give a direct answer of forty to sixty words for featured snippets.
- Keep keyword density low; repeat the phrase only where a reader would expect it.
- Cut filler openers like 'In today's fast-paced world'.
- Write a meta description of 150 to 160 characters that promises a specific answer.

title: Speeches and presentation text
hint: Write speeches, toasts, talks and presentation scripts
text:
- Write for the ear: short sentences under about twenty words.
- Open with a concrete story or number, not 'Thank you all for coming'.
- Give each section one message and repeat the key line once.
- Mark pauses and emphasis in the script; plan about 130 to 150 words per minute.
- Keep slides to keywords and figures; the speaker carries the sentences.
- Close with one thing to think or do, then stop talking.

title: Dialogue and character voice
hint: Write character dialogue, roleplay replies and personas
text:
- Give each character a distinct vocabulary, sentence length and habit of speech.
- Keep the character's knowledge limits; they do not know what the author knows.
- Let subtext carry feeling: the character says less than they mean.
- Answer the other character's last line before advancing the plot.
- Keep replies scene-length unless the user asks for more.
- Do not break character with disclaimers or assistant-style explanations.
- Show reactions in brief physical action, not paragraphs of narration.

title: Journalism and news style
hint: Write news reports, news items and factual articles
text:
- Open the lead with who did what, where and when.
- Use the inverted pyramid: the most important facts first, detail after.
- Attribute every claim to a named source or document.
- Separate reported facts from opinion; label opinion clearly.
- Use no adjectives of judgment such as 'shocking' or 'brilliant'.
- Quote people verbatim and mark any paraphrase.
- Write a neutral headline that matches the lead without sensational words.
